column11: THE US POPULATION-BASED FIGURE, NOT THE DUTCH ONE. Johnson SA, Shouman K, Shelly S et al., 'Small Fiber Neuropathy Incidence, Prevalence, Longitudinal Impairments, and Disability', Neurology 2021;97(22):e2236-e2247 (doi 10.1212/WNL.0000000000012894, PMID 34706972, PMC8641968), the Rochester Epidemiology Project: 'Test-confirmed patients with SFN in Olmsted, Minnesota, and adjacent counties were compared 3:1 to matched controls (January 1, 1998-December 31, 2017)' and 'Ninety-four patients with SFN were identified, with an incidence of 1.3/100,000/y that increased over the study period and a prevalence of 13.3 per 100,000.' 13.3 per 100,000 on the 324,985,539 US residents at 1 July 2017 (Census Bureau Vintage 2019, nst-est2019-alldata.csv) = 43,223
column12: THE NUMBER IN CIRCULATION IS FOUR TIMES THIS AND IS NOT A US RATE. Peters MJH, Bakkers M, Merkies ISJ, Hoeijmakers JGJ, van Raak EPM, Faber CG, Neurology 2013;81(15):1356-1360 (doi 10.1212/WNL.0b013e3182a8236e, PMID 23997150) reports 'The overall minimum prevalence was 52.95 (95% confidence interval 42.47-65.23) cases/100,000', which on the US population would be 172,080. It is a Dutch referral-centre catchment figure from a dedicated small-fibre-neuropathy clinic, not a defined population denominator, and the authors say so: 'These rates probably are an underestimation and are expected to increase in the coming years, since the awareness of SFN is increasing worldwide.' The gap between 13.3 and 52.95 is a diagnosis-rate question, not an epidemiology question, and it is the single largest uncertainty in this layer. Carry 172,080 as the high-ascertainment upside if a scenario needs one, but not as the base

column12: THE TRIAL ASKS FOR MORE THAN IDIOPATHIC AND THE EXTRA IS NOT CUT, SO THIS ROW READS HIGH. NCT06980948 is a 'Safety and Tolerability Study of ST-503 for REFRACTORY Pain Due to Peripheral Neuropathy (Small Fiber Predominant, SFN)'. NO FREE SOURCE PUBLISHES A REFRACTORY SHARE OF SMALL FIBRE NEUROPATHY. What exists is non-quantified narrative with no denominator, single-centre case series already selected for being refractory, or figures for neuropathic pain in general rather than this disease. Nothing is applied rather than inventing a share, and the row says so. A refractory share anywhere in the usual 30% to 50% band would cut this layer by half or more

column12: A BORROWED RATE AND THE WEAKEST ROW IN THIS FILE, for three reasons a human should weigh. (1) Duchenne is a fatal monogenic disease of childhood with a tiny, fully identified, centre-managed population; small fibre neuropathy is a chronic pain disorder of adults managed largely in general neurology and primary care, where a 30,256-patient pool is dispersed across thousands of prescribers. That argues the rate is too high. (2) Against that, the incumbent in refractory small-fibre pain is gabapentinoids and opioids, which is a far weaker standard than Duchenne's. (3) NCT06980948 is Phase 1/2 with 27 participants and a primary outcome of 'Incidence and severity of treatment emergent adverse events (TEAEs)', so the 2027-07 readout buys safety, not an indication. A COMPANY FLAG: the book records this issuer as SGMOQ, Sangamo Therapeutics, primary exchange OTC (the companies table). A move from a national exchange to over-the-counter is material to whether this programme gets funded at all, and a human should establish the issuer's status before valuing the layer
